promptBlocks.text: One continuous handheld take with a five-beat script, a dedicated SETTING block, a PHYSICS clause and a bystander-camera plan. Paste it as written.

tutorialHtml:
DENIZ AKKABAK · SEEDANCE 2.0 TUTORIAL · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

The Grandmother Gambit

Directing a viral street-magic comedy in Seedance 2.0 — a sidewalk card show, an unbeatable grandmother, and one trick that lands exactly where it shouldn't.

A TUTORIAL BY DENIZ AKKABAK · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

MODEL SEEDANCE 2.0 FORMAT 16:9 · 15S · ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE GENRE STREET-MAGIC COMEDY

Street-magic videos go viral on one mechanic: the audience thinks it knows who the show is about, and then it doesn't. This clip runs that reversal twice in fifteen seconds — the performer is upstaged by a grandmother, and the grandmother is upstaged by her own final card. One character sheet goes in as the only reference; everything else, from the yellow cab to the beat of silence before the laughter, is written. Below: the reference, the verbatim prompt, and why the joke lands.

STEP 01

The Reference — One Sheet, One Star

The only attachment is the character sheet: front, profiles, back and a face close-up on a clean white background. It answers the identity question from every angle Seedance might need on a busy sidewalk full of turning heads. Everyone else in the video — the grandmother, the crowd, the pedestrians — is cast entirely by the prompt, which keeps the scene flexible while the star stays locked. Note the parenthesis in the reference block doing quiet, critical work: the sunglasses stay on for the entire video.

REFERENCE 1 — THE CHARACTER SHEET (ATTACH ALONE)

Set Seedance 2.0 to 16:9 and 15 seconds, attach the sheet as the only reference, then paste the prompt below unchanged.

STEP 02

SEEDANCE 2.0 · 16:9 · 15S · ONE CONTINUOUS HANDHELD TAKE

FORMAT: 15s / 16:9 / viral street-magic comedy / single continuous handheld take

STYLE: Realistic amateur iPhone street footage, natural handheld sway, rolling shutter wobble, phone auto-exposure, flat ungraded colors, everything sharp, no cinematic grading, real New York street daylight.

REFERENCES:

Reference 1 = the man: curly dark hair, short beard, black square-framed sunglasses (the sunglasses stay on his face for the entire video), dark overshirt over a grey tee, beige trousers, white-grey sneakers. Preserve his exact face, hair and outfit in every frame.

SETTING: A real New York sidewalk in daylight - brick storefronts, a parked yellow cab, pedestrians passing, honking traffic ambience. The man stands mid-frame performing card magic for a small circle of onlookers.

VIDEO PROMPT:

0-3s: The man fans a deck of playing cards with a smooth flourish and springs the cards from one hand to the other, onlookers filming with their phones.

3-6s: A very old grandmother in a floral coat and headscarf shuffles into the circle, pulls her own deck from her handbag with a smug grin. The man steps back, amused.

6-10s: The grandmother performs a flashy show-off routine - she arcs the entire deck through the air from her left hand to her right in a long controlled card cascade, cards flying in a smooth stream, then ribbon-spreads them across one palm and snaps the spread closed. The crowd whoops.

10-13s: For her finale she flicks a single card hard - it spins through the air, curves back, and smacks flat against her own forehead, sticking dead-center between her eyebrows.

13-15s: She freezes and goes cross-eyed, staring up at the card stuck on her brow, completely deadpan, while bystanders scream and burst out laughing. The man's jaw drops. Hard stop, no fade.

PHYSICS: Cards have real paper weight and spin, the cascade follows a gravity arc, the final card sticks flat to her skin like a harmless suction trick - comedic, no injury, no marks on her skin.

CAMERA: A bystander filming on a phone at chest height, vertical, loose reactive framing, one small step closer during the grandmother's routine, a quick jolt and shaky laugh-shake at the finale, autofocus hunting between the flying cards and faces.

SOUND: Street ambience, traffic, card flutter and crisp snaps, the crowd going oooh during the cascade, a sharp thwip on the throw, one beat of silence, then screams turning into loud laughter, someone yelling NO WAY!

NEGATIVE PROMPT: no cuts, no zoom, no gimbal smoothness, no cinematic grading, no cartoon, no identity change, no face distortion, no distorted hands, no extra fingers, no on-screen text, no captions, no watermarks.

STEP 03

Anatomy — Why the Joke Lands

  1. 1

    The contract

    FORMAT commits to a single continuous take — no cuts to hide behind. For a magic clip that matters double: an unbroken shot is what makes the tricks read as really happening.

  2. 2

    Witness camera

    STYLE and CAMERA cast the phone as a bystander, not a director: reactive framing, autofocus hunting between cards and faces, a laugh-shake at the finale. The camera believing the scene is what makes the viewer believe it.

  3. 3

    Locked star, written world

    Reference 1 freezes the man down to the sunglasses-always-on clause, while SETTING builds the world in text — brick storefronts, the parked yellow cab, honking ambience. Locked identity plus written scenery is the cheapest reliable recipe for street scenes.

  4. 4

    The double reversal

    The five beats are a status game: pro shows off, grandmother out-performs him, grandmother's own finale betrays hers. Comedy structure written as choreography — each beat has a clear physical action and a clear loser.

  5. 5

    The physics clause

    PHYSICS grounds both the skill and the gag: real paper weight, a gravity arc on the cascade, and the final card sticking like a harmless suction trick — no injury, no marks. It keeps the slapstick photoreal and keeps it kind.

  6. 6

    Silence before laughter

    SOUND scripts the comic timing itself: the thwip, one beat of silence, then screams turning into laughter and a yelled NO WAY. That written pause is the difference between an event and a punchline.

  7. 7

    The insurance

    NEGATIVE PROMPT targets this genre's exact failure modes: no cuts and no gimbal smoothness protect the witness illusion, while no distorted hands and no extra fingers protect the one thing card magic cannot survive — broken hands.

THE RESULT

Output — Fifteen Seconds, Two Upsets

Play it back against the script: the take never cuts, the sunglasses never leave his face, the cascade follows a true gravity arc, the card sticks dead-center with a thwip, and the silence holds for exactly one beat before the street erupts. A comedy beat sheet, executed to the frame.

SHUFFLE. UPSTAGE. THWIP.

Write the reversal, and the street writes the laughter.

Swap the cards for a yo-yo, a basketball or a violin: lock one performer with a sheet, write the world around them, and build five beats where the confident one loses twice. The status-reversal skeleton carries any street talent you can script.
